headline: Prisoner swaps, AI jitters and planets we can hear: when is progress real?
teaser: Can a prisoner exchange lead to peace? Is AI spending a bubble? And could we find new worlds by listening instead of looking?

articles.title: Talks Without a Truce: What Can a Prisoner Swap Achieve?
articles.dek: Russia and Ukraine agreed in Abu Dhabi on their largest prisoner exchange of the war, but is a humanitarian deal a first step toward peace or a substitute for it?
paras: After nine months without face-to-face meetings, negotiators from Russia and Ukraine sat down again this week in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates. The two days of talks, which ended on November 11, were mediated by the United States and led on the American side by envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff. Neither President Vladimir Putin nor President Volodymyr Zelenskyy attended; instead, the delegations were headed by Russia's chief negotiator, Vladimir Medinsky, and Ukraine's David Arakhamia. Expectations were modest from the start, and the meeting did not produce a plan to end a war that is now approaching its fifth year. It did, however, produce one concrete result: both sides agreed to a large exchange of prisoners of war.

According to Kushner, the swap will be "the biggest humanitarian release of prisoners" since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. The exact numbers were still being finalized when the talks closed, and Russia's state news agency TASS reported that the exchange should take place within two to three weeks. The delegations also discussed other humanitarian questions, including the return of Ukrainian civilians held in captivity and of children taken from Ukraine during the war. Kushner described the session as "a very tough meeting but a productive one," Zelenskyy called it "constructive and quite substantive," and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said it was "very productive" while warning that a real breakthrough would take time.

Prisoner exchanges are not new in this conflict. In May 2025, after talks in Istanbul, the two countries carried out a 1,000-for-1,000 swap, and in March of this year each side freed 200 prisoners following a meeting in Geneva. Between these headline events, smaller exchanges of 100 to 300 people have taken place every two or three months, according to one analyst quoted by Al Jazeera. What makes the new agreement notable is therefore not the idea itself but its scale, and the fact that it emerged from the first meeting of the three delegations since February.

Supporters of this step-by-step approach argue that humanitarian deals are the most realistic place to begin. When two governments distrust each other deeply, agreeing on something limited and verifiable, such as the number of soldiers to be returned on a particular day, can build a minimum of confidence. Each successful exchange shows that commitments can be kept, and diplomats hope that this record will make harder conversations possible later. Families on both sides also gain something immediate and concrete, regardless of what happens at the negotiating table.

Skeptics, however, point out that swapping prisoners does nothing to resolve the issues that keep the war going. Kushner himself acknowledged that territorial questions will be the hardest to settle, even though he said progress had been made on a framework for security after the war. Neither side has shown a willingness to abandon its core demands, and fighting continues along a front line that has barely moved this year. From this perspective, repeated humanitarian agreements risk creating an impression of momentum while the central disagreements remain untouched.

A further dispute concerns who should be in the room. Russia has long resisted direct European involvement in the negotiations, although Medinsky said after this round that Moscow did not oppose the participation of the European Union, while questioning what the two sides would actually discuss. Ukraine takes a different view. Arakhamia argued that future talks should be multilateral and include Europe, and Zelenskyy said he did not believe European security could be considered without Europe. Representatives of the EU and NATO consulted with the Ukrainian delegation in Abu Dhabi, but they were not formal participants.

The next steps will test which interpretation is correct. Kushner and Witkoff planned to brief Putin in Moscow and then meet Zelenskyy in Dublin, while Arakhamia spoke of "good momentum" toward a solution before the end of the year. If the prisoner exchange goes ahead smoothly, it may strengthen the case that small, practical agreements can open a path to larger ones. If the talks stall again, critics will argue that humanitarian gestures, however valuable to the families involved, cannot substitute for compromise on the questions that matter most. For now, the Abu Dhabi meeting offers a reminder that in diplomacy, progress and stalemate can exist at the same time.

articles.title: Boom, Bubble or Both? Wall Street's Nervous Bet on AI
articles.dek: AI stocks bounced back after a sharp sell-off, reviving the question of whether huge AI spending is a sound investment or a bubble.
paras: On Wednesday, November 11, investors on Wall Street rushed back into the technology stocks they had been selling only days earlier. The S&P 500 rose 1.3% to 7,619.38, almost erasing the losses of the previous week's sell-off and leaving the index within 2.6% of the all-time high it set in October. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite climbed 1.6%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 0.5%. The rebound followed a period of unusual volatility driven by a single question that now hangs over global markets: is the enormous spending on artificial intelligence a sound investment, or a bubble waiting to burst?

The day's biggest winner illustrated both sides of that debate. CoreWeave, a company that rents out the powerful computer chips used to train and run AI systems, saw its shares jump 24.7%. Its third-quarter revenue rose 168% to about $3.7 billion, and it lost less money over the summer than analysts had expected, although its net loss still reached roughly $709 million. The company also raised its revenue forecast for the year and said it expects about $9 billion in customer prepayments and deposits over the next three months. Before Wednesday, however, its stock had fallen by more than 40% in a month.

Other companies connected to AI also recovered. The memory-chip maker Micron gained 11.9%, Broadcom rose 4%, and Nvidia, the world's leading designer of AI chips, climbed 2.9% after losing more than $430 billion in market value over two days earlier in the week. Markets in Asia shared the optimism: South Korea's Kospi index, which is heavily weighted toward chipmakers, rose 2.6%. To optimists, the rebound was a sign that last week's panic had been an overreaction and that demand for computing power remains extremely strong.

Several separate forces had been weighing on these stocks. A worse-than-expected inflation report on Tuesday pushed bond yields higher and raised expectations that the Federal Reserve will increase interest rates, perhaps more than once. Higher rates matter especially for AI infrastructure, because building data centers requires huge amounts of borrowed money; some of CoreWeave's bonds already pay yields above 16%, a sign that lenders see considerable risk. Investors were also concerned that gains by the Democratic Party in last week's midterm elections could lead to new restrictions on AI data centers, which consume vast amounts of electricity and land.

Those who fear a bubble often recall the dot-com era of the late 1990s, when investors poured money into internet companies on the assumption that future profits would justify almost any price. When those profits failed to arrive quickly enough, the Nasdaq lost most of its value between 2000 and 2002. Today's skeptics see familiar signs: companies spending far more on chips and buildings than they currently earn from AI products, and share prices that swing sharply on a single earnings report. The investment firm Baird, for example, downgraded Nvidia this week, citing reduced visibility into data-center forecasts for 2027.

Optimists reply that the comparison is misleading. Unlike many internet start-ups of the 1990s, the largest AI spenders are highly profitable firms, and the demand for computing power is measurable rather than hypothetical, as CoreWeave's billions in prepayments suggest. Some analysts even argue that physical limits could help established leaders. Morgan Stanley noted that shortages of land, power and construction capacity for data centers may protect the market share of dominant chip suppliers, since newcomers would struggle to compete for the same scarce resources.

Both interpretations may contain some truth. A technology can be genuinely transformative while its stock prices still run ahead of reality, as the internet itself proved: the dot-com crash ruined many investors, yet the internet went on to reshape the global economy. For ordinary observers, the lesson of this week is less about predicting the next move in share prices than about recognizing what drives them. Interest rates, electricity supplies and political decisions may matter as much to the future of AI as the brilliance of the technology itself.

questions.highlight: A technology can be genuinely transformative while its stock prices still run ahead of reality, as the internet itself proved: the dot-com crash ruined many investors, yet the internet went on to reshape the global economy.

articles.title: Listening for Planets: How Gravitational Waves Could Reveal New Worlds
articles.dek: A NASA study suggests the future LISA observatory could find planets around pairs of dead stars by 'hearing' them in gravitational waves, but the method has never been tested.

sources.name: NASA Science: LISA formally adopted by ESA

paras: For three decades, astronomers have discovered planets beyond our solar system mainly by watching light. They look for the tiny dip in brightness when a planet passes in front of its star, or for the slight wobble in a star's light caused by an orbiting planet's gravity. A new NASA study proposes a very different approach: detecting planets not through light at all, but through ripples in space itself. According to two papers published in The Astrophysical Journal and described by NASA on November 10, a future space observatory called LISA could reveal an entirely new population of worlds.

Those ripples are gravitational waves, disturbances in the fabric of space-time that Albert Einstein predicted in 1916. They are produced when massive objects accelerate, for example when two dense stars orbit each other at high speed. Because the waves are extraordinarily weak by the time they reach Earth, scientists needed almost a century to build instruments sensitive enough to detect them. Ground-based observatories finally recorded the first gravitational wave in 2015, a signal from two colliding black holes, and the discovery was soon recognized with a Nobel Prize.

LISA, the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna, is designed to go much further. Led by the European Space Agency, which formally adopted the mission in 2024, it is scheduled to launch in the mid-2030s, with NASA contributing telescopes, other hardware, and engineering and science support. LISA will consist of three spacecraft flying in a triangle whose sides each measure about 2.5 million kilometers. By firing lasers between them, it will be able to detect changes in distance smaller than the width of a helium atom, which is precise enough to sense the slow, steady waves given off by pairs of stars in our galaxy.

The new research focuses on one kind of pair: double white dwarfs. A white dwarf is the dense, Earth-sized core left behind when a star like the Sun runs out of fuel. Scientists estimate that the Milky Way contains about 10 million pairs of white dwarfs orbiting each other in less than an hour, and LISA is expected to pick out around 10,000 of them individually. If a planet circles such a pair, its gravity will slightly disturb the pair's motion. That disturbance would add faint extra signals, called sidebands, at frequencies just above and below the pair's main signal. The idea resembles the radial velocity method, which finds planets by measuring how they make their stars wobble, except that LISA would read the wobble in gravitational waves rather than in starlight.

The concept itself is not entirely new; the Japanese astrophysicist Naoki Seto first suggested it in 2008. What the new papers add is a detailed estimate of which planets could realistically be found, and a plan for confirming them. The second paper examines how the James Webb Space Telescope, whose infrared instruments can detect the extra heat a planet gives off, might follow up LISA's discoveries. In a test case set 500 light-years away, Webb could detect a planet about five times as massive as Jupiter, whereas LISA, under ideal conditions, could detect one smaller than Jupiter.

If such planets exist, they would be remarkable. No planet has ever been found orbiting a pair of white dwarfs, and any that survive there must have endured the violent late stages of their stars' lives, when the stars swelled and shed much of their material. Finding them would help scientists understand whether planetary systems can outlive their stars, a question with obvious relevance to the distant future of our own solar system, since the Sun is expected to become a white dwarf in several billion years.

There are, however, reasons for caution. The method has never been tested, and the most impressive estimates depend on ideal conditions that real data rarely provide. Signals from thousands of white dwarf pairs will overlap, making faint sidebands difficult to separate from noise. Moreover, the observatory will not launch for roughly a decade, and large space missions are often delayed. Even so, the study shows how a new kind of instrument can change the questions astronomers are able to ask. Just as telescopes once extended human vision, gravitational-wave detectors may allow scientists, in effect, to listen to the universe.

speak.p: Some people think governments should spend large amounts of money on space science, such as new telescopes and observatories. Others think the money should be used to solve problems on Earth first. Which view do you agree with? Use specific reasons and examples.
speak.hint: State your view → reason 1 (knowledge, inspiration, new technology or urgent needs on Earth) + example → reason 2 + example → short conclusion.

write.p: Professor: NASA scientists say a future space observatory, LISA, could find planets by detecting gravitational waves, but it will not launch until the mid-2030s and the method has never been tested. Missions like this take decades and cost billions. In your view, is it worth investing in long-term science projects whose results are uncertain and may arrive many years later? Why or why not? (Aisha says: Yes. Many important discoveries were unexpected. Gravitational waves themselves took a century to detect, and that work produced new technology and a Nobel Prize. Science needs patience.) (Lucas says: I am not so sure. When results are uncertain and far away, the money might do more good in projects that solve problems now, such as climate monitoring or medical research.)
steps: Choose a side: worth it, or not worth it.
Give one reason linked to knowledge and technology, or to urgent needs.
Add an example, such as the 2015 detection or a present-day problem.
Respond to Aisha or Lucas, then conclude in one sentence.

words.ex: The International Space Station can orbit Earth about sixteen times a day.

words.def: having a lot of mass packed into a small space
words.ex: Lead is a dense metal, so even a small piece feels heavy.

words.def: able to detect or respond to very small changes
words.ex: This microphone is so sensitive that it can pick up a whisper across the room.

words.def: exact and accurate in every detail
words.ex: The recipe gives precise measurements for every ingredient.

questions.q: Which of the sentences below best expresses the essential information in the highlighted sentence in paragraph 7? Incorrect choices change the meaning in important ways or leave out essential information.

Too extreme: the problem is finding faint sidebands, not detecting the pairs at all.
